paper_title: VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Token

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Video matting, the task of extracting foreground objects with pixel-level precision from video, is fundamental component of video editing applications such as background replacement [56, 12, 36], visual composition [10, 51], and relighting [4, 36, 46, 8]. Producing convincing composites in these settings requires alpha mattes that capture fine structures such as hair strands and motion-blurred edges, and that remain temporally consistent across the entire video. Recent video matting methods leverage priors from video object segmentation models [19, 53]. However, these methods still rely on dedicated matting annotations and offer limited zero-shot generalization, with most existing methods restricted to human portraits due to the scarcity of matting labels for other categories. more recent line of work instead leverages video diffusion priors [27, 13], transferring generative knowledge obtained from internet-scale pretraining to close the traintest gap that arises when models are trained only on synthetic matting data. In particular, VideoMaMa [27] demonstrates that mask-to-matte diffusion model trained on synthetic data alone can generalize to non-human categories and to in-the-wild video footage. However, applying diffusion-based matting to real videos exposes fundamental limitation that hinders general video processing. Diffusion backbones are computationally heavy and cannot process arbitrarily long sequences in single forward pass; existing methods are therefore chunk-based, handling only 624 frames at time. As result, even ordinary videos must be split into multiple chunks and processed sequentially. When each chunk is matted independently from its coarse mask guidance, the resulting mattes drift across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency, as illustrated in Figure 1 (b). The root cause is the inherent ambiguity of coarse mask guidance: single binary mask admits many plausible fine-grained refinements at object boundaries, and independently processed chunks settle on different ones. In this work, we present novel mask-guided diffusion-matting framework designed for long, highresolution video. At its core, we represent the two guidance modalities, the RGB frames and the coarse mask, as separate token streams alongside the noisy matte tokens, and let them interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention. This design replaces the channel concatenation used in prior U-Net-based diffusion matting [27] and preserves each modalitys distinct structure. The high-frequency RGB texture carries hair and edge cues, while the binary mask provides coarse but spatially anchored foreground extent, and attention adaptively composes the two at every layer and spatial location. As result, the model leans on RGB at object boundaries where the mask is unreliable, and on the mask in the interior where it confidently localizes the foreground. We instantiate this on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [34, 45] with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [42], which naturally accommodates diverse resolutions and frame counts. To resolve the chunk-boundary inconsistency described above, we introduce novel pair of learnable token embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, new conditioning interface for consistent video matting. The preserve token marks frame whose guidance is already fine matte, previously generated or ground truth, and tells the model to keep it as reference. The refine token marks frame with only coarse mask and asks the model to refine it into fine matte consistent with the preserve-tagged references via DiTs full self-attention. We employ these tokens in sliding-window inference scheme in which each chunk overlaps few preserve-tagged frames with the previous chunk, so that already-generated mattes propagate across chunk boundaries and maintain local temporal consistency. To further guard against error accumulation over long sequences, we additionally supply globally reliable matte as reference anchor at every chunk through the same preserve token, without any additional training. We validate our framework through extensive experiments on standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild footage. Our method outperforms existing video matting approaches on VideoMatte [28], YoutubeMatte [53], and V-HIM60 [19] in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and 2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-video matting where prior diffusion-based methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries. The same preserve mechanism also gives users direct control at inference time, for example to interactively correct erroneous outputs by re-tagging specific frames as refine while keeping trusted neighbors as preserve. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. mask-guided diffusion-matting framework with token-level guidance representation, where the RGB frames and the coarse mask are kept as separate token streams adaptively composed by full spatio-temporal self-attention, rather than fused via channel concatenation as in prior works. novel preserve and refine token mechanism that enables chunk-consistent matting through sliding-window inference with overlap-based propagation, complemented by globally shared reference anchor that prevents error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. State-of-the-art performance on standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild longvideo footage, with substantial gains in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency over prior diffusion-based methods that process video chunk-wise.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Video matting. Video matting methods can be broadly categorized into auxiliary-free and auxiliaryguided approaches [33, 16]. Auxiliary-free methods [29, 21, 23] typically focus on portrait matting, restricting their applicability to human-centric scenarios. Auxiliary-guided approaches relax this restriction by accepting additional conditioning at the cost of an extra annotation. Trimap-guided methods [17, 40] require manual trimap annotations and cannot easily leverage modern segmentation models such as the SAM family [22, 35, 3]. More recent mask-guided methods reduce this burden by accepting only coarse binary mask. MaGGIe [19] decouples target tracking from matting but struggles to generalize to in-the-wild videos, while MatAnyone [53, 52] propagates target-assigned mattes through memory-augmented architecture trained on dedicated matting datasets such as VM800 [53] and VMReal [52]. Despite these advances, all of these methods remain constrained by predominantly synthetic and human-centric training data, leaving in-the-wild generalization to non-human categories largely unsolved. Diffusion priors for perception. Diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining have been transferred to dense perception tasks. Marigold [20] pioneered this direction by adapting Stable Diffusion [38] for depth estimation, and the same recipe extends to range of video perception tasks [1, 41, 15, 50], with more recent works [49, 57] extending it to DiT-based backbones. Diffusion long-video inference. Diffusion backbones, however, are computationally heavy and limited to short chunks, so applying them to long videos requires chunk-wise inference scheme. ChronoDepth [41] and DepthCrafter [15] adopt sliding-window inference with overlapping frames between adjacent chunks for local temporal smoothness, but offer no global anchor against drift. parallel line of work tackles this through auto-regressive generation [18, 5, 55, 30, 9, 54, 32], where each chunk is conditioned on the previous chunk via causal attention with KV-cache reuse. While effective for free-form video generation, this hidden-state propagation does not naturally compose with explicit external conditioning such as guide mask. Our work instead propagates fully-formed reference mattes between chunks through the preserve token, keeping each chunk fully conditioned on its own user-supplied mask. Diffusion-based video matting. In the matting domain, recent diffusion-based methods transfer video diffusion priors to video matting using only synthetic data. The auxiliary-free GVM [13] and the mask-guided VideoMaMa [27] both demonstrate that this prior generalizes to non-human categories and in-the-wild footage, but both inherit the chunk-wise inference limitation of prior diffusion-based perception models. VideoMaMa, the closest mask-guided baseline, additionally fuses RGB, mask, and noise via channel concatenation, entangling the guidance modalities and limiting fine-detail recovery. Our work departs from this design by representing the two guidance modalities as separate token streams, and by introducing the preserve and refine tokens that maintain chunk-wise consistency through globally shared reference anchors and overlap-based local smoothing.

sections.content: Figure 2: Overview of the VideoMaMa++ training and inference. (Top) During training, RGB frames are paired with either binary mask or the ground-truth alpha matte as guide input, encoded into separate token streams by frozen VAE encoder E, and tagged with refine token (R) or preserve token (P). The DiT processes both modes jointly within single clip, supervised against the ground-truth matte. (Bottom) At inference, long videos are processed in sliding-window manner. Each chunk receives the refine token on its non-overlapping frames and the preserve token on its overlap frames, which carry the previous chunks predicted matte. globally selected reference anchor frame is additionally supplied as preserve input to every chunk, providing stable anchor that prevents error accumulation across the sequence.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview
sections.content: Video matting is mathematically defined by the alpha compositing equation, It = αtFt + (1 αt)Bt, = 1, . . . , T, (1) where denotes the frame index, is the total number of frames in the video, It is the observed image at frame t, Ft is the foreground, Bt is the background, and αt [0, 1] is the alpha matte representing pixel-level opacity. Unlike binary segmentation masks {0, 1}, alpha mattes capture fine-grained details such as hair strands, motion blur, and semi-transparent regions, which are critical for realistic video compositing. We adopt mask-guided formulation that decomposes video matting into two subproblems: foreground tracking and boundary refinement. Tracking target object across video is itself demanding task, and entangling it with matte generation forces single model to simultaneously localize objects and resolve pixel-level matting. By conditioning on binary mask, we decouple these two challenges and allow our model to focus on generating fine-grained matting details such as hair strands and motion blur, while inheriting localization capabilities from off-the-shelf segmentation models [35, 3, 7, 6]. We design an end-to-end pipeline for long-video matting that takes video and single user prompt on the first frame as input, and produces temporally consistent alpha matte across the entire sequence. The pipeline operates in three stages, illustrated in Figure 2. First, we obtain per-frame foreground signal by propagating the user prompt across all frames using an off-the-shelf video segmentation model such as Segment Anything [35, 3]. Second, the resulting binary mask track is passed to our Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbone together with the RGB frames to generate fine-grained alpha 4 mattes (Section 3.2). Finally, long sequences are handled by chunk-wise inference scheme equipped with preserve and refine tokens (Section 3.3), which propagates information across chunk boundaries to maintain temporal consistency throughout the video.

sections.title: 3.2 Repurposing Diffusion Transformer for Video Matting
sections.content: Video matting annotations are scarce and limited in quantity and category coverage. Generalizing to real-world footage therefore requires strong prior over natural video content. We build our framework on video DiT [34, 45] backbone, which provides rich generative prior learned from internet-scale video pretraining and offers several architectural properties well-suited to video matting. The input video , the guide mask track , and, during training, the ground-truth alpha matte α are each encoded into the latent space by shared, frozen VAE encoder E, producing zV , zM , and zα respectively. We sample Gaussian noise ϵ (0, I) with the same shape as zα, and concatenate zV , zM , and ϵ along the token dimension as input to the DiT backbone: (cid:0)concat(zV , zM , ϵ)(cid:1), ˆzα = FDiT (2) where FDiT() denotes our adapted DiT and concat() denotes concatenation. Unlike UNet-based matting models [27, 2] that fuse the three modalities along the channel dimension, our token-level concatenation lets each modality occupy its own token stream and preserves modality-specific information throughout the network. The final alpha matte video is obtained by decoding the predicted latents through the VAE decoder, ˆα = D(ˆzα). We initialize from the pretrained DiT [45] and, instead of its original flow-matching objective, supervise the decoded predictions directly in pixel space (see Appendix A). Although training follows the standard multi-step schedule, we find single denoising step at inference sufficient to produce high-quality mattes, and adopt it as our default for efficiency.

sections.title: 3.3 Preserve and Refine Tokens
sections.content: The formulation above operates on single clip, while video matting in practice requires handling long sequences. DiT backbones are computationally heavy and cannot process long videos in single forward pass. natural solution is chunk-wise inference, where the video is split into fixed-length clips and each clip is processed independently. However, when each chunk is refined from its guidance in isolation, the resulting mattes drift across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. To address this, we introduce two learnable token embeddings, preserve token and refine token, which assign each frame per-frame mode that determines whether its matte is carried through unchanged or generated from coarse guidance. The preserve token marks anchor frames whose alpha mattes should be retained, while the refine token marks frames that should be converted from coarse guidance into fine-grained alpha mattes. DiTs full self-attention propagates information from preserve frames to refine frames, yielding mattes that remain consistent across chunks. Why not auto-regressive diffusion? We chose to propagate fully-formed reference mattes through the preserve token rather than reuse the previous chunks key-value (KV) cache as in auto-regressive diffusion approaches [18, 55]. Hidden-state propagation implicitly turns the model into propagationbased matting framework, where each chunks prediction is determined more by the previous chunks internal state than by its own mask guidance. This re-entangles localization and fine-detail recovery, the two subproblems we explicitly decoupled by adopting mask-guided conditioning. The preserve token instead exposes the previous chunks contribution as an explicit alpha matte, so each chunk remains fully grounded in its own mask guidance while still receiving long-range temporal context through self-attention. Training. We train both tokens jointly within single clip. For each training clip, we randomly select subset of frames as preserve frames, replace their guide input with the ground-truth alpha matte, and add the preserve token embedding to those frames. The remaining frames receive the refine token together with the standard binary mask guide input. The model is supervised against the ground-truth matte at all frames through the pixel-level supervision, learning to reconstruct the supplied matte at preserve frames and to generate fine-grained mattes from coarse guidance at refine frames. sections.title: 3.4 Temporally Consistent Inference
sections.content: We deploy the preserve and refine tokens at inference through two complementary mechanisms: sliding-window scheme that propagates mattes between adjacent chunks for local consistency, and reference anchor that supplies globally reliable matte at every chunk to prevent long-range drift. Sliding window. At inference, we apply sliding-window scheme in which consecutive chunks share an overlap region. The overlapping frames receive the previous chunks predicted matte as input together with the preserve token, so that their mattes are passed through unchanged, while the remaining frames receive the guide signal together with the refine token. Although the preserve token is applied only to the overlap frames, DiTs full attention allows them to condition the generation of every other frame in the chunk, transferring temporal context across the chunk boundary and producing chunk-consistent mattes. Reference anchor. The sliding-window scheme alone is vulnerable to error accumulation, since corrupted overlap frame, e.g., due to occlusion, tracking drift, or other video artifacts, propagates through the preserve token to all subsequent chunks and cascades local failures through the rest of the video. To prevent this, we introduce reference anchor, globally reliable frame whose matte is supplied as preserve input alongside the local overlap frames at every chunk, providing stable, error-free signal that the model can attend to throughout inference while the overlap frames continue to carry short-range temporal context. Crucially, this capability emerges directly from the preserve token without any additional training: because the preserve token already learns to treat its inputs as anchors, any user-supplied matte can serve as an anchor for the rest of the video. This design gives users explicit control over which frame anchors the inference. By default, we reuse the matte predicted at the first chunk as the reference anchor throughout the video, which we find sufficient for most sequences. When the first frame is unreliable due to heavy occlusion, motion blur, or partial visibility, the user can instead select later frame with cleaner foreground appearance as the reference, allowing the entire sequence to be conditioned on the most informative anchor available.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We build VideoMaMa++ on top of the Wan 2.1 (1.3B) [45] model, training on combination of image and video matting datasets. To preserve the generative prior, we adapt the DiT to the video matting task using LoRA [14] rather than fine-tuning the full backbone. Training uses 3-frame clips at 1024 1024 resolution, which provides sufficient capacity for both spatial detail and temporal modeling. At inference, we process the video in chunks of 6 frames with 2-frame overlap between consecutive chunks, where one of the overlap frames is the reference anchor. Although the training and inference settings differ in both frame count and chunking behavior, the model generalizes across them due to RoPEs [42] relative position encoding, which removes the dependence on absolute resolution and clip length present in fixed positional embeddings.

sections.content: We evaluate VideoMaMa++ on three benchmarks: VideoMatte240K [28], YouTubeMatte [53], and V-HIM60 (Hard) [19]. All mask-guided methods, including ours, receive identical guidance masks 6 Figure 3: Long-video temporal consistency. Qualitative comparison between VideoMaMa++ and other methods. The comparison methods exhibits visible flickering at chunk boundaries or struggles to capture fine-grained details, while VideoMaMa++ produces smooth transitions across chunks while still capturing fine-grained details that emerge in later chunks. produced by single procedure (Algorithm 1). The binarized first-frame ground-truth matte prompts SAM3 [3] on duplicated first frame (frames {0, 0, 1, 2, . . . }), and SAM3 propagates it across the video, so every guidance mask, including that of the first frame, is SAM3 prediction rather than the binarized ground truth, and no method receives privileged mask. For one YouTubeMatte sequence, sheet of paper that belongs to the foreground enters mid-video, so all methods share track initialized at later frame in which the paper is visible; VideoMaMa++ remains the best method under first-frame initialization as well (Appendix E). As reported in Table 1, VideoMaMa++ achieves the best performance across all metrics on every benchmark. The improvements are particularly pronounced on Gradient [37] and dtSSD [11], which respectively measure spatial boundary sharpness and temporal smoothness. The Gradient gains confirm that the DiT-based generative prior recovers fine-grained boundary detail more accurately than prior mask-guided methods, while the dtSSD improvements indicate that the preserve and refine token mechanism produces temporally consistent mattes despite chunk-wise inference. We provide further analysis of discontinuities at chunk boundaries in Appendix F.

sections.title: 4.3 Qualitative Evaluations
sections.content: We compare VideoMaMa++ against representative video matting baselines, including MGM in-thewild [33], MaGGIe [19], MatAnyone 2 [52], and VideoMaMa [27], on in-the-wild videos. Figure 3 shows long videos that diffusion models (VideoMaMa and ours) cannot process in single chunk. As shown in the figure, the comparison methods either fail to capture fine-grained details or produce flickering results across chunks that are inconsistent over the full video. In contrast, VideoMaMa++ produces mattes that retain fine-grained boundary detail consistently throughout the sequence and remain stable across distant frames, demonstrating that our DiT-based generative prior, combined with the preserve and refine token mechanism, generalizes effectively to long-form footage well beyond the length seen during training. We refer the reader to the supplementary material for additional comparisons that more clearly demonstrate temporal consistency in motion. We further quantify this observation with an annotation-free test for chunk-boundary discontinuities (Appendix F), which detects spikes in the frame-to-frame matte change that recur at chunk seams. With both models run at identical seams, VideoMaMas matte change spikes at seams in-the-wild clips, whereas VideoMaMa++ stays at chance level. We further corrupt the input of the anchor frame (Table 3b) with poor guidance mask (erosion or dilation), horizontal motion blur on the RGB frame, or real occluder composited over nearly the entire subject, whose region is also removed from the guidance mask (Appendix H). Because the anchor is the models own first-frame prediction, the degraded anchor matte propagates to all later chunks. Nevertheless, performance degrades only marginally under every corruption. Effect of preserve token at chunk boundaries. We design targeted experiment to verify that the preserve and refine tokens produce consistent mattes across chunk boundaries. Using chunk size of 6 with an overlap of 2 frames, each overlap frame is generated twice: once as part of the preceding chunk and once as part of the following chunk. We measure the discrepancy between these two predictions for the same frame, which directly reflects how much the matte drifts when the model crosses chunk boundary. The two settings differ only in how the overlap frames are treated by the second chunk: w/o preserve regenerates them independently from the coarse mask guidance, whereas w/ preserve marks them with the preserve token and conditions on the matte produced by the preceding chunk. To isolate the effect of the preserve token, the reference anchor is disabled in both settings. As reported in Table 4, w/ preserve reduces both MAD and Gradient discrepancy by large margin, confirming that the preserve token effectively transfers cross-chunk information and yields mattes that align across chunk boundaries rather than drifting into independently chosen refinements. Robustness to mask generators. To evaluate the robustness of our model to diverse binary mask sources, we measure performance on V-HIM60 [19] using XMem [7], Cutie [6], SAM2 [35], and SAM3 [3] as binary mask generators in Table 5. The results show that the model maintains consistent performance across all mask generators, demonstrating its robustness to the choice of binary mask input. Beyond the choice of generator, the model also tolerates local mask errors: when the guidance mask is wrong on individual frames of chunk, such as missing thin structures or drift under motion blur, cross-frame attention to neighboring frames recovers the matte. If the tracker instead locks onto wrong object for an entire sequence, the matte follows that track, limitation shared by all mask-guided methods. Continuous guidance via SAM logits. We investigate replacing the binary guide mask with SAMs raw logit map, which preserves the soft confidence information discarded by binarization (Figure 5). The structures most affected by this collapse, such as hair strands, thin wires, and motion-blurred edges, exhibit below-threshold logits that are removed entirely once the mask is binarized. We replace the guide mask track in Section 3.2 with SAM logit map, encoded by the same VAE into latent that substitutes for zM in Eq. 2, and retrain the model end-to-end with this logit conditioning rather than swapping inputs only at inference. As reported in Table 6a, the logitconditioned variant outperforms its binary counterpart across all four metrics, confirming that soft confidence carries signals critical for fine-detail recovery. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce VideoMaMa++, diffusion transformer model that leverages generative priors for robust video matting, overcoming data scarcity. VideoMaMa++ introduces preserve and refine tokens that enable temporally consistent matting on long videos, addressing fundamental limitation of diffusion-based approaches confined to short clips. We demonstrate that VideoMaMa++ achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks while producing fine-grained, temporally consistent results on long in-the-wild videos. An annotation-free analysis further shows that our chunk-wise inference exhibits no measurable discontinuity at chunk boundaries, unlike VideoMaMa processing chunks independently. Nevertheless, VideoMaMa++ is more computationally demanding than feed-forward models and, like all mask-guided methods, depends on the upstream mask track; reducing the DiT inference cost and benchmarking temporal smoothness on real footage are promising future directions. We believe VideoMaMa++ provides scalable framework bridging the gap between short-clip generation and real-world long-video applications.

sections.title: Appendix Overview
sections.content: This supplementary material provides additional details on implementation, evaluation, and qualitative results that could not be included in the main paper due to space constraints. The document is organized as follows: Section provides additional implementation details, including the training configuration and the list of datasets used to train VideoMaMa++. Section presents qualitative results for the interactive refinement experiment, illustrating how VideoMaMa++ progressively improves its own predictions across iterations through the preserve and refine token mechanism. Section reports zero-shot evaluation of VideoMaMa++ on image matting benchmarks, demonstrating that our model generalizes effectively beyond video to single-image settings. Section discusses annotation noise in the AM-2K benchmark and explains why MAD-T provides more reliable measure of matting quality than MAD on this dataset. Section describes the guidance-mask generation protocol shared by all mask-guided methods and reports single evaluation exception on the YouTubeMatte static_0017 sequence, where SAM3 [3] must be re-initialized at later frame to capture an object that enters the scene partway through the video, together with results under first-frame initialization Section introduces an annotation-free test for chunk-boundary discontinuities, which quantifies temporal consistency on in-the-wild videos without ground truth, and validates it on YouTubeMatte. Section reports the computational cost of VideoMaMa++ and prior methods, including per-stage runtime breakdown and end-to-end throughput with mask generation. Section details the reference-anchor experiments, including the anchor-refresh setting and the corruption protocol used to test robustness to degraded anchor. Section discusses the limitations of this work: its dependence on the upstream mask track, and the absence of video matting benchmark that can rigorously evaluate temporal smoothness on real-world footage. Section discusses the positive and negative societal impacts of mask-guided video matting.

sections.title: H Reference Anchor Analysis Details
sections.content: This section details the reference-anchor experiments of Table 3, all conducted on V-HIM60 [19]. Anchor choice and refresh. The first frame may not be representative of later frames. We therefore replace it as the anchor with random frame or the last frame of the first chunk, which leaves performance nearly unchanged across all metrics. Because the foreground may also change in appearance over long sequences, we further re-anchor to recent frame every 3 chunks. V-HIM60 sequences contain substantial pose, scale, and appearance variation, yet refreshing yields nearly identical quality to the default setting, so first-frame anchor does not become stale on this benchmark. Refreshing nevertheless remains available at negligible cost for footage whose appearance changes more drastically. Corruption protocol. We corrupt the input of the first frame, which serves as the anchor, rather than the propagated matte. Because the anchor is the models own first-frame prediction, corrupted input yields degraded anchor matte that is propagated to all later chunks. We consider three corruptions: Poor guidance mask. We erode (under-segmentation, E) or dilate (over-segmentation, D) the first-frame guidance mask using grayscale morphology with square kernel of {5, 21} px. Motion blur. We apply horizontal motion-blur kernel of {7, 15, 25} px to the first-frame RGB (B), so the model must matte motion-blurred appearance. Occlusion. We composite real animal foreground from AM-2K [25] over the subject using its ground-truth matte, enlarging it until at least 99% of the subject is covered, and zero the occluded region of the guidance mask so that it remains consistent with the now-invisible subject (Occ.). We exclude the corrupted first frame from evaluation, so the metrics measure how the degraded anchor propagates to the rest of the video. This matters most under occlusion, where the input RGB and the ground-truth matte of the first frame disagree. It is also why the clean baseline in Table 3b differs slightly from the main results: the only difference is the excluded clean first frame. 20 Results. Across all corruptions, performance degrades only marginally relative to the clean baseline. Full occlusion is the most severe case, followed by motion blur and poor guidance masks, and larger kernels generally lead to slightly larger degradation. Even with fully occluded anchor, the model remains close to its clean-anchor performance, indicating that degraded anchor has only limited effect on the rest of the video.

sections.title: I Limitation
sections.content: Dependence on the mask track. VideoMaMa++ deliberately separates tracking, delegated to mask generator such as SAM3 [3], from matting, so its robustness is bounded by the quality of the mask track. Errors confined to individual frames of chunk, such as missing thin structures or drift under motion blur, can be corrected through cross-frame attention to neighboring frames or through interactive refinement (Section B). However, if the tracker locks onto the wrong object for an entire sequence, the matte follows that wrong track. This limitation is shared by all mask-guided matting methods. Evaluating temporal smoothness on real video. key limitation of this work, and of video matting research more broadly, is the absence of benchmark that can rigorously evaluate temporal smoothness on real video. Existing benchmarks [28, 53, 27] are constructed by compositing per-frame foregrounds onto random backgrounds, which provides accurate per-frame ground truth but does not capture the temporal dynamics of naturally captured footage. As result, temporal consistency on real-world videos is still largely assessed qualitatively. The annotation-free seam test of Section quantifies one specific failure mode, discontinuities at chunk boundaries, without ground truth. However, it measures neither per-frame accuracy nor flicker within chunk, and it applies only to methods that process video in chunks, so it cannot compare the overall temporal behavior of arbitrary methods. Developing benchmark with reliable ground-truth temporal smoothness, ideally captured rather than composited, remains an open problem for the community.

sections.title: J Societal Impact
sections.content: Positive Societal Impact. Our mask-guided video matting framework can substantially benefit creative industries, education, and communication. By reducing the manual effort required for highquality video matting, the method lowers the barrier to professional-grade video production, enabling independent creators, educators, and small studios to produce polished content without specialized expertise or costly proprietary software. In film and visual effects, it can accelerate labor-intensive rotoscoping workflows, allowing artists to focus on creative decisions rather than frame-by-frame manual labeling. The technology also improves the quality of background replacement in video conferencing and virtual classrooms, supporting remote collaboration and accessibility-oriented applications such as isolating speakers or interpreters in educational content. Negative Societal Impact. Despite these benefits, high-quality video matting can be misused. As core component in video manipulation pipelines, improved matting may facilitate the creation of more convincing deepfakes and manipulated media, contributing to misinformation and the erosion of public trust in video evidence.
